full_judgment:
Ahsanuddin Choudhury, J.-In this appeal by special leave the point for consideration. is Whether the G. R. Case No. 255 of 1973, pending in the Court of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (N), Barisal in which occurrence took place on 4.8.1973 but charge-sheet was submitted on 20.7.1974 and cognizance was taken on 31.8.1974 under President's Order No. 50 of 1972 (after its repeal on 9.2.1974 by the Special Powers Act XIV of 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) can be tried under President's Order No. 50 (herein after called P.O. 50) as a pending case within the meaning of section 36(2) (b) of the Act and by virtue of section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act. 

 2. The aforesaid case was started on a first information report lodged by one Haji Shamsul Haque Bepari at Mehandiganj Police Station, Barisal alleging that on 4.8.1973 five persons armed with deadly weapons such as pistol and knives attacked his brother Saiduzzaman while he was in his Fair Price Cloth Shop and brutally murdered him. The police after investigation submitted charge-sheet against the accused on 20.7.1974 under Sections 147/148/149/302/109, penal code read with Article 2(4) of P.O. 50. The accused were taken in to custody. Their prayer for bail was rejected, both by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate as well as by the Sessions Judge, Barisal. 

 3. The accused moved the High Court Division for quashing the aforesaid proceeding on the ground that after repeal of P.O. 50 by the Act on 9.2.1974, the instant case in which charge-sheet was not submitted before 9.2.1974 could not be continued under P.O. 50 inasmuch as the saving clause in Section 36(2) (b) of the Act has provided for the continuance of only the pending cases under the repealed statute namely, P.O. 50. The High Court Division did not uphold that contention. The High Court Division has held that by virtue of section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act any investigation or legal proceeding started under the repealed statue would not be affected by the subsequent repeal of the said statute unless a different intention appears in the repealing statute. It has also held that there is nothing to show that the Legislature did not intend to keep alive any other proceeding except the pending cases as mentioned in section 36(2) (b) of the Act. 

 4. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned counsel for the appellants argued in support of the appeal. Mr. Rafiqul Huq and Mr. Moinul Hossein, learned counsel on permission sought by them also addressed us on the point of law involved in this appeal. Mr. Fazlul Karim contended that the High Court Division misconstrued the provisions of the saving clause in section 36(2)(b) of the Act inasmuch as after repeal of P.O. 50 by the Act on 9.2.1974 proceedings in the instant case in which charge sheet was not submitted before 9.2.1974 cannot be continued and tried by the Special Magistrate or the Special Tribunal under P.O. 50 since the Act by the saving clause in section 36(2)(b) has specifically provided for the continuance of only the pending cases be-fore the Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal under P.O. 50. It was urged that in view of the saving clause as regards continuance of only the pending cases under P.O. 50, the legislature did not intend to keep alive any other proceedings started for offences committed under P.O. 50 before its repeal and pending investigation by the police even after the repeal as those proceedings were not cases pending before any Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal as contemplated under section 36(2)(b) of the Act. In support of his argument the learned counsel relied upon a decision of Appellate Division in the case of solicitor, Bangladesh Vs. A T. Mridha reported in 26 D.L.R. 17 to show that a case which was pending with the police for investigation could not be considered to be a case before a court so as to be a pending case under P.O. 50 before a competent Tribunal as contemplated in section 36(2)(b) of the Act. He also relied upon two decisions of the High Court Division a one in the case of Tozammel Hossain Vs. The State reported in 27 D.L.R. 36 and the other in the case of A. T. Mashood Vs. The State reported in the same volume at 93 in support of his contention that the cases in which charge-sheet was not submitted under P.O. 50 before 9.2.1974 no charge-sheet under P.O. 50 could be submitted thereafter and those cases cannot be tried under P.O. 50 by a Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal. 

 5. In Mridha's case the points considered by the Appellate Division were whether the order of detention passed by the sub-Divisional Magistrate under clause (3) of Article 13 of P.O. 50 was a judicial order passed by a court or it was an administrative order and whether in the facts and circumstances of that case the order passed by the High Court Division quashing the proceedings pending with the police for investigation could be sustained. With regard to the first point it was held by the Appellate Division that the order of detention passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate was an administrative order which was passed during the stage of enquiry or investigation by any police officer designated for that purpose, so the said order was not subject to revision by the High Court Division under sections 435 and 439 of the code of criminal procedure. So far as the second point was concerned the Appellate Division after taking into consideration the fact that the case was under investigation by the police held that there was no case before the Special Magistrate under P.O. 50 as before submission of charge-sheet under Article 4(1) of P.O. 50 and taking cognizance of the case thereof, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate does not function as a special Magistrate under P.O. 50, so the order passed by the High Court Division under section 561(A) of the Criminal Procedure Code quashing a proceeding which was not before any court but under investigation by the police was held to be not sustainable in law. It was, therefore, submitted that the instant case which was pending with police for investigation till 9.2.1974 was not a case before the special Magistrate or special Tribunal and as such it was not a pending case before the court and cannot be tried under P.O. 50. The learned Attorney-General submitted that in view of the decision in Mridha's case it cannot be said that the present case before us was a case pending before the special Magistrate or special Tribunal on 9.2.1974. It was however pointed out that the decision in Mridha's case was given in April, 1974 whereas P.O. 50 was repealed in February, 1974. Before the Appellate Division it was not contended that on account of repeal of P.O. 50 on 9.2.1974 the case pending thereafter with the police for investigation could on longer be considered as one under P.O. 50 and that the said case was destroyed by the repeal of P.O. 50, rather the Appellate Division set aside the order by which the High Court Division quashed the proceeding under investigation. It was, therefore, argued that the Appellate Division by setting aside the order of quashment of the proceeding under investigation virtually approved of the investigation of the case under P.O. 50 by the police. It was thus submitted that it could not be said that the alleged offence under investigation under P.O. 50 in which charge-sheet was not submitted till 9.2.1974 was destroyed due to the repeal of P. 0. 50 and that the said offence ceased to be one triable by the special Magistrate or by the special Tribunal as by the saving provisions only cases pending before the appropriate court on 9.2.1974 were saved. 

 6. As regards two aforementioned decisions of the High Court Division, the case of A. T. M. Mashood reported in 27 D.L.R. 93 is an earlier one. It appears that on a first information report lodged at Balaganj P.S. by a Circle Inspector, Sadar (C), Sylhet, a case was started under sections 395 and 397 of the Penal Code read with P.O. 50. A criminal Revision being No. 364 of 1974 was filed for quashing the said case on the ground that no cognizable offence was disclosed, that P.O. 50 was repealed from 9th February, 1974 and that no charge sheet having been submitted before that date alleging any offence under P.O. 50, the impugned proceedings could not be said to be a pending case before any Special Magistrate or Tribunal within the meaning of section 36(2)(b) of the Act. Nevertheless, the High Court Division refused to quash the proceedings. It observed that since P.O. 50 stood repealed from 9.2.1974 and no charge-sheet was submitted before that date alleging any offence under the aforesaid order, the proceedings could not be a pending case within the meaning of section 36(2)(b) of the Act so as to be continued under the provisions of the repealed P.O. 50 although under whatever other law, the accused might be proceeded against. The other decision is in the case of Tozammel Hossain Sardar and others reported in 27 D.L.R. 36. It appears that on a first information report, a case was started on 7. 10. 73 under section 302/34 read with P.O. 50. In this case also no charge-sheet could be submitted under P.O. 50 before 9.2.1974, the date on which P.O. 50 stood repealed. So it was contended before the High Court Division that inasmuch as there could be no trial of the accused before the special Magistrate or special Tribunal constituted under P.O. 50, the case should be quashed. The prayer for quashing of the case was refused and it was held that since no charge-sheet under P.O. 50 was submitted till 9.2.1974 no charge-sheet could be submitted under P.O. 50 after the aforesaid date. Consequently, the trial of the accused could not be held before the special Magistrate or special Tribunal constituted under P.O. 50. it was however, observed that if a prima facie case was made out against the accused under section 302/34 and the charge-sheet was submitted against them under the aforesaid sections they might be tried before a competent court under ordinary jurisdiction. 

 7. It may be noted there that the same bench of the High Court Division which decided the above two cases took a different view in Criminal Miscellaneous case No. 84 of 1974, Shyamal Chandra Das and others Vs. The State in which the prayer for grant of bail of the accused was made. In that case the accused were proceeded against for an offence under the Arms Act read with P.O. No. 50 under which the offence under the Arms Act was declared to be a grave offence. In the said case the occurrence took place on 6th of February, 1974 and no charge-sheet could be submitted before 9th February, 1974. The contention before the High Court Division was that the case in which the investigation against the accused was still in progress was not a case pending within the meaning of section 36(2) (b) of the Act and as such it could not be tried under P.O. 50 by the Special Magistrate or the Special Tribunal. In this case the High Court Division took into consideration the provisions of clause (e) of section 6 of the General Clauses Act along with the provisions of the saving clause in section 36(2)(b) of the Act and held that section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act would govern the situation and in spite of the repeal of P.O. 50 the investigation or proceeding started under P.O. 50 before its repeal would be continued under the provisions of the repealed order. Having taken this view the bail was refused. It may be pointed out that the provisions of section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act were not considered in the earlier two decisions reported in 27 D.L.R. 36 and 93. The decision in Criminal Misc. Case No. 84 of 1974 has been followed by other Benches of the High Court Division in criminal revision case No. 470 of 1974 in the case of Sabjee Ali Vs. The State and in Criminal Revision case No. 584 of 1974 in the case of A. K. Rabbani alias Salam versus the State which were sought to be quashed on the ground that those cases were not kept alive by the re-pealing Act. In all those cases it has been held that in the absence of any clear intention of the legislature to the contrary in the repealing Act the cases or proceedings under investigation of offences under P.O. 50 would be a case under P.O. 50 by virtue of section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act as if P.O. 50 was not repealed and the Repealing Act had not been passed. Taking this view, the prayer for quashing of these cases was rejected by the High Court Division, It may, however, be mentioned that the judgments in those cases namely, Criminal Miscellaneous case No. 84 of 1974, Criminal Revision case No. 470 of 1974 and Criminal Revision case No. 584 of 1974 are said to be yet unreported. Be that as it may, it is obvious that except in two earlier decisions in cases of Tozammel Hossain Sarder and A. T. M. Mashood reported in 27 D.L.R. 36 and 93 the High Court Division has taken a consistent view in the later cases that in the absence of any clear intention to the contrary in the repealing statute the proceedings purported to be under P.O. 50 for offences alleged to have been committed prior to 9.2.1974 and lying with police for investigation would come within the ambit of P.O. 50 by virtue of section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act. 

 8. As regards the arguments made by Mr. Rafiqul Huq we are obliged to observe that the argument advanced by him was not something much different from what was urged by Mr. Fazlul Karim Mr. Rafiqul Huq, the learned counsel argued that since clause (b) of section 36(2) of the Act has made express provisions regarding cases under P.O. 50 which were pending on 9.2.1974, the legislature must have intended not to keep any proceedings other than pending cases under P.O. 50 alive. According to him clause (b) of section 36(2) of the Act clearly shows that the intention was to make proceedings other than pending cases dead. 

 9. Mr. Moinul Hosain, the learned counsel, in course of his argument, recalled the circumstances under which P.O. 50 was enacted and repealed. He submitted that P.O. 50 was enacted on May 22, 1972. Making special provisions for the suppression of certain offences he sought to point out that those offences were already offences under certain other penal laws but under P.O. 50 those offences were declared to be scheduled offences and offences of grave nature which were made exclusively triable by special Magistrates or special Tribunals constituted as special forum under clause (2) of Article 3 of P.O. 50. It is thus evident that not only new offences were created under P.O. 50 but new forum was also created for trial of those offences. The learned counsel urged that after a lapse of certain period since the enactment of P.O. 50 there was a strong public demand for repeal of P.O. 50 as the object and reasons for which P.O. 50 was enacted were no longer there. Further more an impression grew among the public in general that the continuance of an enactment like P.O. 50 should not be allowed to remain any longer as a statute inasmuch as this law was being abused by way of harassment to citizens of the country. So the legislature could not but repeal P.O. 50, but not withstanding the repeal, the legislature by way of abundant caution considered it expedient to enact in the repealing Act a saving clause namely, clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 36 to save only those cases which were pending before any special Magistrate or special Tribunal and no other proceedings. 

 "Section 36(2)(b) reads all cases pen-ding. before any special Magistrate or special Tribunal appointed or constituted or deemed to be appointed or constituted under the Bangladesh Scheduled Offences (Special Tribunal) Order 1974 (P.O. No. 50 of 1972) immediately before the commencement of this Act shall be tried and disposed of by such special Magistrate or special Tribunal, and all matters in connection with such cases shall be regulated in accordance with the provisions of the said order, as if the said order had not been repealed by this Act." 

 12. It is now to be seen whether in view of the specific provisions for a continuance of the pending cases under P.O. 50 in the saving clause of the Act, the cases pending investigation by the police for offences under P.O. 50 up to the date of its repeal are to be taken as dead or destroyed or will be proceeded with in view of the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. 

 13. It was argued with reference to the saving clause quoted above that the intention of the Legislature being so clear and manifest with respect to the cases protected by the saving clause, there is no scope for application of 6 of the General Clauses Act so as to bring the proceedings started for offences allegedly committed under P.O. 50 prior to its repeal and pending with police for investigation in which charge-sheet could not be submitted before repeal of P.O. 50 within its ambit. It was further argued that the special forum constituted under P.O. 50 for trial of scheduled offences ceased to exist from 9-2-1974 except as provided in section 36(2)(b) of the Act. so no special forum being available to take cognizance of and try those cases under P.O. 50, they may at best be tried by the court of ordinary jurisdiction in as much as those offences prior to their having been declared scheduled offences and offences of grave nature under P.O. 50 were offences under respective penal laws namely penal code and Arms Act etc. It is thus apparent that the approach of Mr. Hosein to the question involved in this case is not for total destruction of the offences but for change of forum of trial after repeal of P.O. 50. 

 14. The learned Attorney General, it seems, rightly argued that even though the cases pending before the special Magistrate or the special Tribunal have been specifically mentioned, it does not mean that the legislature intended to destroy the scheduled offences alleged to have been committed till the date of repeal of P.O. 50 and in respect of which investigation was at the hand of the police, not it can be said that the legislature intended that the trial of those offences after repeal of P.O. 50 would be held by a different forum. It was submitted that when a law is enacted, the pros and cons thereof as well as its relative effect with respect to the other connected laws are deeply considered by the legislature namely, the law makers. It will therefore be too much to say that the legislature while enacting the saving clause (2)(b) of section 36 were unaware of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. It was therefore urged to look to the consequences of repeal of P.O. 50 upon the proceedings pending investigation thereunder with reference to the relevant provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. Before doing so we think it will be useful to state briefly the circumstances necessitating the enactment of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, section 6 corresponds to section 38(2) of the English Interpretation Act, 1889. Prior to the enactment of the Interpretation Act of 1889, the effect of repeal of one statute by another without any express saving was to obliterate the repealed Act as completely from the records of the parliament as if it had never been passed and it must be considered as a law that never existed except for the purpose of those actions which were commenced, prosecuted and concluded whilst it was an existing law, vide Craies on Statute law, 5th Edition pages 322-23, such being the effect of repeal tinder the law of England obtaining before 1889, a repeal without any saving clause used to destroy not only all rights, privileges, obligations, liabilities, penalties and causes of action accrued under the repealed Act but also all proceedings pending on the date of repeal, except actions wholly concluded and ripened into vested rights by judgments before the repeal, vide Crawford on Statutory Constriction, 1940, edition pages 599-600 and 657-658 with a view to preventing such consequences resulting from the repeal of a statute, a practice grew in England to insert a saving clause in the repealing statute so as to preserve the rights and liabilities etc. accrued under the repealed statute and the proceedings instituted under that statute before its repeal. In order to dispense with the necessity of inserting a saving clause in each repealing Act, section 38(2) was inserted in the English Interpretation Act of 1889. The then Central Legislature of India followed suit and enacted the General Clauses Act in the year 1897, inserting therein section 6 corresponding to section 38(2) of the aforesaid English Act. It is, therefore, quite clear that one of the important purposes of section 6 of the General Clauses Act is to protect rights and liabilities already accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment. Relevant provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act are as under: 

 15. Where there is a repeal of an enactment the consequences laid down in section 6 of the General Clauses Act which are saving provisions will follow unless a different intention appears. The line of enquiry would be not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. That being so, section 6 does not admit of any strictly technical interpretation which may frustrate its very purpose. This leads us to consider whether in the present case any right or liability accrued or incurred wider P.O. 50 before its repeal shall be deemed to have been destroyed. It is settled by now that when a statute is repealed either wholly or in part, the repeal forthwith attracts section 6 of the General Clauses Act. This being the situation all prosecutions under the repealed Act which were pending on the date of its re-peal would be saved and must be proceeded with notwithstanding the repeal of that Act unless an express provision was otherwise made in the repealing Act. In support of this view reliance may be placed in the case of Balish Vs. Rangachari Income Tax Officer, reported in A.I.R. 1949 (S.C.) 701. In that case, appellant Balish, a cinema actor was prosecuted for submission of a false Income Tax return under section 52 of the Income Tax Act 1922. The alleged offence was committed when the Income Tax Act 1922 was in force but the prosecution was started after its repeal by the Income Tax Act, 1961. The repealing Act contained a saving clause in section 297 (2). Under that section provisions were made keeping alive some proceedings which were pending under the repealed Act but the provisions in the saving clause did not specifically cover the appellants case. It was, therefore, contended that the parliament had intentionally dropped such a case but the said contention was rejected. Ramaswami, J. who delivered the judgment observed as follows: 

 "The principle of this section is that unless a different intention appears in the repealing Act, any legal proceeding can be instituted and continued in respect of any matter pending under the repealed Act as if that Act was in force at the time of repeal. In other words, whenever, there is a repeal of an enactment the consequences laid down in section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless, as the section itself says, a different intention appears in the repealing statute. In the case of a simple repeal there is scarcely any room for expression of a contrary opinion. But when the repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject the court would undoubtedly have to look to the provisions of the new Act, but only for the purpose of determining whether they indicate a different intention. The question is not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an entertain to destroy them. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, therefore, will be applicable unless the new legislation manfests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the sections. Such incompatibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the relevant provisions of the new statute ad the mere absence of a saving clause is by itself not material. In other words, the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act will apply to a case of repeal even if there is a simultaneous reenactment unless a contrary intention can be gathered from the new statute." 

 16. The learned counsel for the appellants on the other hand, referred to the case of the public prosecutor, Government of Pandechary Vs. Abdul Aziz Khan reported in 1910 Mad. 311 to show that in respect of application of section 6 of the General Clauses Act and the saving section of any special enactment it should be considered whether the new enactment manifests an intention to destroy all matters except what has been specifically kept alive. In the case under reference the respondents were appointed Liquidators of a company under the Company's Act (Act VII of 1913). They were prosecuted under the said Act on 6-8-1966 for non- submission of return although Act VII of 1913 had been repealed by Act (1 of 1956). Of course, sections 645-657 of Act (I of 1956) made provisions of saving certain cases started under the repealed Act. Section 648 specifically saved a prosecution started by a liquidator or ordered by the court under the repealed Act. But the prosecution against the liquidator-respondent was started on a private complaint by the Registrar of the companies. So a question arose whether the said prosecution was saved by section 6 of the General Clauses Act as it was not saved by section 648. It was held that the prosecution was not saved. The learned Judges observed as follows: 

 17. The learned counsel for the appellants placed relianace also on the case of Qudrutullah Vs. Bareilly Municipality reported in A.I.R. 1974 (S.C.) 396. The facts are that the defendant-appellants had for several years been collecting `Tahabazare dues from a market Patelganj under contracts from the Municipal Board, the last of which according to the plaintiff was executed on 19-11-1944. Defence case was that on expiration of the term of that contract a fresh contract was entered into on 31-12-1947 substantially repeating the same terms and conditions but on the basis that the said contract did not materialise into a biding one for want of Government approval, the plaintiff by a notice asked the defendants not to realise the market dues. The defendant having continued to realise the market dues a suit was filed praying for putting the plaintiff in absolute proprietary possession after dispossessing the defendants from certain sheds and passages situated in bazar Patalganj. The defendant in the suit pleaded the status of a tenant and protection as a tenant under the U. P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act (U.P. Act III) of 1947. But the said Act was repealed by U.P. Urban (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 (Act XIII of 1972) which entitled the Board to an ejectment decree. It was contended that the fight that accrued to the defendant under the earlier Act could not be taken away by its repeal since the later Act was not in terms a retrospective one. It was held that though factually it was correct to say that section 43 of the later Act was not made retrospective, nevertheless, on the repeal of the Act the disability which the plaintiff suffered, disappeared and he was entitled to enforce his cause of action. Hence the protection against ejectment was no longer available to the defendant. It was held that the general principle that an enactment which is repealed is to be treated, except as to transaction passed and closed, as if it had never existed. It was, however, observed that the operation of this principle is subject to any saving which may be made expressly or by implication by the repealing enactment. (Vide Halsbury's Laws of England Vol. 36 para 714). It is to be noted that the principle which has been laid down in the decisions considered above namely, A.I.R. 1970. Madras 311 and A.I.R. 1974 (S.C.) 396 does not militate against the principle laid down in A.T.R. 1969 (S.C.) 701. we do not see how these decisions help the appellants with a view to show that the offences alleged to have been committed under P.0.50 till the date of its repeal and proceedings in respect thereof pending with the police for investigation were destroyed. 

 18. The provisions of clauses (c) and (e) of section 6 of the General Clauses Act are clear enough to show that any investigation or legal proceedings started under the repealed statute will not be affected by the subsequent repeal of the said statute. It thus difficult to accept the contention that the legislature did not intend to keep alive any other proceedings under P.O. 50 except pending cases as mentioned in section 36(2)(b) of the Act. Simply because section 36(2)(b) is silent on other cases it does not follow that the parliament intended to destroy them. There is nothing in the language in clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 36 of the Act from which it cannot be concluded that only the cases pending before the Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal in its restricted meaning have been saved. If, however, that restricted view is taken then the offence under P.O. 50 committed immediately before its repeal will go unpunished which, we think, could not be the intention of the legislature. It is true that specific mention of the pending cases was only made in the repealing Act but it does not appear from the repealing Act that the cases pending for investigation which are covered by section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act would be deemed to have been destroyed. There is nothing to show from the provisions of the repealing Act that any intention-contrary to the saving provisions of section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act has been expressed in the Act with a view to show that the legislature intended to destroy the Offences committed under P.O. 50 up to the date of its repeal but did not come before the court through submission of charge sheet under Article 4(i) of P.O. 50. In the case of A Maleque Vs. Abdur Rahman PLD (1967) 19 DLR 318-PLD 1968 Dacca 96 Sayem J. as his lordship then was, observed at page 105: 

 19. Mr. Moinul Hossain's contention that on repeal of P.O. 50 the forum, that is, the courts of the Special Magistrate and the Special Tribunal having ceased to exist except as provided under section 36(2)(b) of the Special Powers Act for the purpose of pending cases and that if proceedings other than pending cases are allowed to continue, there would be an anomalous situation because after the repeal there would be no Tribunal or Special Magistrate to take cognizance of any offence under the repealed Act has got no substance. If it is found that in spite of the repeal, proceedings will continue under the repealed Act, then all matters in connection with such proceeding shall also be governed in accordance with the provisions of the said order, that is P.O. 50 as if the said order has not been repealed by the Act. On this point reference may be made to a decision reported in P.L.D. 1970 (S.C.) 254 which corresponds 22 DLR (SC) 155 in the case of Sona Vs. The State. While considering the effect of section 6 of the General Clauses Act it was observed that repeal of the Act shall not affect pending proceedings under it, moreover proceedings may be continued and punishment may be imposed as if the repealing Act has not been passed. 

 20. It needs reiteration that the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act must come into operation in case of repeal of an enactment and in that view of the matter the proceedings in respect of offences of P.O. 50 pending investigation with the police must be covered by the provisions of section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act. 

 21. In the result the appeal must fail and it is hereby dismissed. The instant case i.e. G.R. Case No. 255 of 1973 in which charge-sheet has been submitted and cognizance has been taken under P.O. 50 after its repeal is to be tried by the Special Magistrate or the Special Tribunal as the case may be.
